q: Does the sub-Poissonian lethal-lesion result survive when the primary DSB induction distribution is over-dispersed (negative binomial, as expected at high LET), rather than treated as a deterministic initial condition X0?
basis: The paper assumes X0 is a fixed initial count and derives Fano(Y) < 1 from clustering + repair dynamics alone. At high LET, primary DSB counts per cell are empirically and mechanistically over-dispersed (spatially clustered on sub-nuclear scales; see Friedland et al. 2017 track-structure work; Ballarini & Ottolenghi 2005). If the input X0 ~ NegBin(mu, phi) with phi >> 1, the output variance of Y inherits an input-driven component that may swamp the paper's -delta(t) contraction. The paper does not test this and its 'sub-Poissonian' headline could be misleading in the very regime (heavy ions, boron capture, proton Bragg peak) where LUCID users care most.
next_steps: Rerun the existing SSA (code/gsm2_model.py) with X0 sampled from NegBin(mu=100, phi in {1,2,5,10}) instead of a fixed X0=100. Report Fano(Y) at t=1.5 as a function of phi. If Fano(Y) crosses 1, identify the phi_crit at which the paper's headline flips. Cost: <1h CPU, $0. This is a strict extension of the existing single-parameter replication; no new code beyond a 5-line input distribution change.

q: How well does the linear-noise approximation hold in the high-clustering regime (large b_tilde_K or small r), where the MME non-linearity dominates and higher-order van Kampen corrections may become O(1)?
basis: The paper's Sec. 4 numerics fix (r, a, b_tilde) = (4, 0.1, 0.01), a regime where clustering rate b_tilde * xbar^2 <= 100 * 0.01 = 1 is small compared to r*xbar <= 400 for most of the trajectory. The van Kampen expansion is a leading-order asymptotic in 1/sqrt(K); the paper does not quantify when the next-order (Kramers-Moyal or 1/K) correction becomes important. LNA is known to fail (i) as xbar -> 0 (paper's own caveat, our C4) and (ii) when the non-linearity in the drift is comparable to the diffusion coefficient. Regime (ii) is unexplored.
next_steps: Parameter sweep: fix (a, r) = (0.1, 4) and scan b_tilde_K in {0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0} at fixed x0=100. Compare SSA and LNA Fano(Y) at t=1.5 and Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between the SSA and LNA marginals of Y at t=0.7. Report the b_tilde_K at which KS > 0.05 (a reasonable failure threshold). Also run x0 in {10, 30, 100, 300} at the paper's default rates to expose the small-x0 quantized regime where LNA fails from below. Cost: <2h CPU, $0.

q: Do the paper's model rate constants (r, a, b) have an identifiable mapping to any published radiobiological observable (foci-count histograms, cell-survival curves, complex-DSB fractions)?
basis: The paper picks (r, a, b_tilde) = (4, 0.1, 0.01) 'for illustration' with no reference to a fit against experimental data. Three constants over one observable (survival at one dose) is underdetermined; the constants are also correlated in their effect on Fano(Y) (increasing r reduces mean Y; increasing b increases variance component from clustering). Without an identifiability analysis (Fisher information matrix, profile likelihoods, or a joint fit to a dose-response + foci-histogram dataset), the model is a plausibility argument rather than a predictive tool. This is the gap between 'the paper's math is right' (which we have verified) and 'the paper's model is useful for LUCID predictions' (which is not established).
next_steps: Two probes. (a) Compute the Fisher information matrix of Fano(Y) with respect to (log r, log a, log b_tilde) via finite differences on the moment ODE (Eq. 16) and report its condition number - if kappa > 10^4 the constants are effectively unidentifiable from Fano(Y) alone. (b) Fit (r, a, b_tilde) to a public gamma-H2AX foci-count dataset (Rothkamm & Lobrich 2003 or Barnard et al. 2013 supplementary tables); report best-fit constants, 95% profile-likelihood intervals, and residual QQ plot. Cost: (a) 30 min CPU + Fisher analysis, $0; (b) 1-2 days for data acquisition + fit, $0 if datasets are public.

q: How is the sub-Poissonian conclusion modified by realistic two-phase repair kinetics (fast NHEJ + slow HR/backup) or by cell-to-cell heterogeneity in the rate constants?
basis: The paper assumes a single time-constant sub-lethal repair rate r. Real DSB repair is well-established as bi-exponential (Rothkamm & Lobrich 2003; Metzger & Iliakis 1991): a fast NHEJ component (t_1/2 ~ 10-30 min) and a slow component (t_1/2 ~ 4-8 h). Similarly (r, a, b) are near-certainly heterogeneous across cells (cell-cycle phase, chromatin state, individual variation). The paper's headline could either strengthen or weaken under these extensions: heterogeneity of r across a population is a classical mechanism for over-dispersion (mixture of Poissons is over-dispersed), so it might push Fano(Y) above 1 even when each individual cell is sub-Poissonian.
next_steps: Extension of the same SSA. (a) Split X into X_fast and X_slow with rates (r_fast=8, r_slow=0.5) at a 70/30 initial split; rerun and compute Fano(Y). (b) Cell-to-cell heterogeneity: draw r_i ~ LogNormal(log 4, sigma) for sigma in {0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0} across 20000 independent cells; compute population Fano(Y) at t=1.5. Report the sigma at which population Fano crosses 1. Cost: 2-4h CPU, $0. Interpretation: this quantifies how much of the 'lethal lesions are sub-Poissonian' story is a per-cell statement vs a population statement.

q: Does the moment closure at second order (LNA / linear FPE) systematically underestimate the tail probability P(Y >> ybar), and if so, what does that imply for extrapolating from Fano(Y) to cell-survival (which is dominated by the tail P(Y >= 1)) at low dose?
basis: The LNA gives a Gaussian marginal for Y with mean ybar(t) and variance c_vv(t). At the paper's parameter set, c_vv(t=1.5) ~ 7.65 and ybar(t=1.5) ~ 11.26; the Gaussian tail P(Y > ybar + 3 sigma) ~ 0.00135, whereas the true CTMC (a compound counting process with a clustering term) is known to have heavier tails than Gaussian for such reaction networks (Kurtz 1978; Anderson & Kurtz 2015). For radiobiology this matters: at low dose the interesting quantity is P(Y=0) (cell survival), which the LNA computes from the Gaussian CDF at 0. If the true P(Y=0) differs from the Gaussian prediction by even a factor of 2, cell-survival curves derived from the moment ODE alone will be miscalibrated at exactly the low-dose regime where LNSS (linear-no-threshold vs threshold) debates live.
next_steps: From the existing 20000 SSA paths, tabulate the empirical CDF of Y at t=1.5 and compare against the Gaussian CDF with matched (mean, variance). Report (a) KS distance, (b) empirical vs Gaussian P(Y=0) and P(Y >= 20), (c) Anderson-Darling p-value. If KS > 0.05 or tail ratios > 2, escalate to a saddle-point or system-size correction estimate of the tail. If the discrepancy is significant, quantify how it propagates to a Poisson-of-lethal-lesions cell survival S(D) = P(Y=0 | dose D) and how much the LNA-derived survival curve differs from the SSA-derived one at low doses (0.1 - 1 Gy). Cost: 1h CPU for the empirical tests, $0; ~4h for the survival extrapolation, $0.
